notes.title: Concept - The Multilayer Perceptron
notes.scope: The MLP as the base neural network: neurons, weights, biases, the affine-then-nonlinearity stack, the forward pass, and universal approximation. IN: layer structure, why nonlinearity is essential, forward-pass math and FLOP count. OUT: how it is trained (link The Training Loop, Backpropagation), specific activations (link Activation Functions), the transformer FFN's exact shape (link 03).
key_points: A layer computes h = act(Wx + b); with no nonlinearity a stack collapses to a single linear map W3*W2*W1 -- the nonlinearity is the entire source of expressivity, and stacking Linear layers with no activation is a silent underfitting bug

Universal Approximation Theorem (Cybenko 1989, Hornik 1991): one hidden layer of sufficient width approximates any continuous function on a compact set -- but the required width can be exponential; depth is exponentially more parameter-efficient (Telgarsky 2016, Eldan-Shamir 2016)
Parameter count of a layer is d_in*d_out + d_out; the weight matrix dominates, bias is negligible; forward FLOPs are ~2*params per input token
The XOR problem (Minsky and Papert 1969) is not linearly separable and killed the single perceptron; a hidden layer solves it -- the historical hinge that stalled and then revived the field
The 'MLP' is exactly the position-wise FFN block inside every transformer (usually 4x expansion then projection back); understanding it here transfers directly to 03
Bias-variance intuition at the surface: width/depth increase capacity; why huge nets still generalize is the deep story (link Generalization in Deep Learning)
links: Concept - Matrix Multiplication as the Atom of Deep Learning

notes.title: Concept - Loss Functions for Neural Networks
notes.scope: The objective a network minimizes and how it shapes gradients: MSE/MAE/Huber for regression, cross-entropy for classification, label smoothing, and the softmax+cross-entropy fused gradient. IN: which loss for which task, why CE beats MSE for classification, label smoothing, loss-at-init diagnostics. OUT: the information theory of cross-entropy (link 01 Entropy and Cross-Entropy), preference/RL objectives (link 06), the softmax function itself (link Softmax).
key_points: Cross-entropy loss = -sum(y_i * log(y_hat_i)); paired with softmax its gradient w.r.t. the logits is the clean y_hat - y, which is exactly why softmax+CE dominates classification

MSE through a sigmoid output has gradient proportional to sigmoid'(z) which vanishes when the unit saturates -- the concrete reason CE replaced MSE for classification (fast learning even when badly wrong)

Label smoothing (Szegedy et al. 2016): replace hard target 1.0 with 1-eps (typ. eps=0.1); improves calibration and stops logits growing unboundedly, but Muller et al. 2019 show it erases inter-class structure and can hurt as a distillation teacher
Loss-at-init sanity check: for C balanced classes CE ~ ln(C) at step 0 (e.g. ln(50257) ~ 10.82 for GPT-2 vocab, ln(1000) ~ 6.9 for ImageNet) -- a canonical first diagnostic before touching the model
Reduction matters: mean vs sum vs per-token changes the effective learning rate by batch/sequence length; the masked-loss token-count bug is a classic silent SFT error (link 06)
Huber/MAE trade robustness to outliers against slower convergence; regression heads matter for value/reward models (link 06 Reward Models)

notes.title: Concept - Backpropagation
notes.scope: Reverse-mode automatic differentiation applied to neural nets: the chain rule over the computational graph, forward activations cached for the backward pass, and per-op vector-Jacobian products. IN: the algorithm, the DAG, memory cost, matrix-form local gradients, why reverse-mode. OUT: the optimizer update (link SGD, Adam and AdamW), each layer's specific gradient (in that layer's note), gradient checkpointing/recompute at scale (link 04/08).
key_points: Backprop is reverse-mode autodiff: one forward pass caches activations, one backward pass propagates the adjoint dL/dv via local vector-Jacobian products in reverse topological order; each node needs only its local Jacobian, never the full one

Cost is ~2x the forward pass (the 'backward is 2x forward' rule of thumb); memory is dominated by retained forward activations, which must live until consumed in backward (link 08 Memory Math for Transformers)

Why reverse-mode not forward-mode: one scalar output (the loss) and millions of inputs (params) -> reverse costs O(1) passes vs O(#params) for forward-mode; forward-mode wins only for few-input many-output Jacobians

Matrix form is the whole game: for Y = X W, the backward is X_bar = Y_bar W^T and W_bar = X^T Y_bar -- two matmuls, so the backward pass is also matmul-bound (link 01 Matrix Multiplication as the Atom of Deep Learning)

Failure modes: gradients vanish or explode multiplicatively across depth (link Vanishing and Exploding Gradients); an in-place op or a .detach() silently severs the graph and zeroes upstream gradients
Backprop computes exact analytic gradients; finite-difference gradient checking (relative error < 1e-5) is the canonical unit test for a hand-written backward
Non-obvious: activation recomputation (gradient checkpointing) trades compute for the activation-memory wall -- the same idea FlashAttention exploits (link 08)
links: Concept - Matrix Multiplication as the Atom of Deep Learning
Snippet - A Minimal Training Loop in PyTorch

notes.title: Concept - The Training Loop
notes.scope: The canonical optimization loop and its correct ordering: forward -> loss -> backward -> clip -> optimizer step -> zero grad, plus epochs/steps/batches, train vs eval mode, gradient accumulation and clipping. IN: the loop skeleton, each step's role and ordering hazards, effective batch size. OUT: distributed/at-scale loop mechanics and LR schedules (link 04), each optimizer's math (link its note).
key_points: The five-line core: opt.zero_grad(); loss = f(x,y); loss.backward(); clip_grad_norm_(...); opt.step(). loss.backward() ACCUMULATES into .grad by design (for RNNs/accumulation), so forgetting zero_grad silently sums gradients across steps -- the #1 beginner bug
Effective batch = micro-batch * grad-accum steps * data-parallel world size; gradient accumulation trades more steps for less peak memory at fixed effective batch
Gradient clipping by global norm (max_norm ~1.0 is the folklore default) tames spikes; in mixed precision you must UNSCALE before clipping and stepping (link 04 Mixed Precision Training)
model.train() vs model.eval() flips BatchNorm running-stat updates and Dropout; forgetting to switch leaks train-time noise into eval or corrupts running stats (link Breakdown - Batch Normalization)
zero_grad(set_to_none=True) is the modern default: it skips a memory write and frees grad tensors, slightly changing semantics (None vs 0) that some code depends on
First debugging move is always overfit-a-single-batch to ~0 loss (link Playbook); the loop is where most 'model' bugs actually live
Non-obvious: put the LR-schedule step and the optimizer step in the right order (scheduler after optimizer in PyTorch >=1.1) or you silently skip the first LR value
links: Snippet - A Minimal Training Loop in PyTorch
Playbook - Debugging a Neural Network That Won't Train

notes.title: Concept - Softmax
notes.scope: The softmax function turning logits into a distribution: definition, numerical stability, temperature, the Jacobian, and the softmax+cross-entropy fused gradient. IN: max-subtraction stability, log-sum-exp, temperature scaling, saturation pathologies. OUT: sampling parameters at inference (link 07), attention's use of softmax (link 03), the loss objective (link Loss Functions).
key_points: softmax(z)_i = exp(z_i)/sum_j exp(z_j); it is invariant to adding a constant to every logit, so subtract max_j(z_j) first to prevent exp() overflow -- the mandatory numerically stable form
log-softmax is computed via the log-sum-exp trick, never as log(softmax(...)); PyTorch fuses log_softmax + nll_loss into cross_entropy for exactly this stability reason
Jacobian d s_i / d z_j = s_i*(delta_ij - s_j); composed with cross-entropy it collapses to the clean y_hat - y (link Loss Functions, Backpropagation)

Temperature T divides logits before the exp: T->0 approaches argmax, T->inf approaches uniform; the same knob controls sampling sharpness (link 07) and distillation soft targets (link 06 Knowledge Distillation)
Softmax saturates: a large logit gap drives the winning probability to ~1 and its gradient to ~0, producing logit blow-up and attention entropy collapse (link 18 Attention Sinks)

The softmax bottleneck (Yang et al. 2018): factoring an N x V log-probability matrix through a d-dim hidden state caps its rank at d, structurally limiting the output distribution's expressivity (link 18)
Non-obvious: logits are only defined up to an additive constant per row, so raw logit values are meaningless in isolation -- only differences matter (relevant to the logit lens in 14)
links: Concept - Loss Functions for Neural Networks

notes.title: Concept - Activation Functions
notes.scope: Pointwise nonlinearities: sigmoid/tanh, ReLU and its variants, GELU/SiLU, their derivatives and pathologies, and why smooth gated activations won in transformers. IN: the functions, gradients, dead-neuron and saturation failure modes, exact-vs-tanh GELU. OUT: gated GLU/SwiGLU FFN variants (link 03), the softmax (link Softmax), full-batch optimization dynamics (link Edge of Stability).
key_points: Sigmoid and tanh saturate: their derivatives peak at 0.25 and 1.0 and decay to 0 in the tails, so deep stacks vanish gradients -- the pre-2010 wall on network depth

ReLU max(0,x) has derivative 0 or 1 and no positive-side saturation; it made deep nets trainable (Nair-Hinton 2010, Glorot et al. 2011) but suffers 'dying ReLU' -- a unit pushed permanently negative gets zero gradient forever and never recovers
Leaky ReLU / PReLU / ELU / SELU add a negative-side slope to keep gradients alive; gains are usually marginal, SELU targets self-normalizing nets (with LeCun init)

GELU x*Phi(x) (Hendrycks-Gimpel 2016) and SiLU/Swish x*sigmoid(x): smooth, non-monotonic dip just below 0; default in BERT/GPT. The tanh approximation of GELU differs from exact GELU by ~0.1% but is a real cross-implementation reproducibility trap
Detection: track the fraction of dead units and activation histograms per layer; a layer with >90% zeros post-ReLU is dying and usually signals too-large LR or bad init
Non-obvious: GELU's edge over ReLU is small and often within noise -- it persists largely by convention inherited from BERT/GPT rather than a decisive mechanistic win
links: Concept - Floating Point for Deep Learning

notes.title: Concept - Stochastic Gradient Descent and Momentum
notes.scope: SGD, mini-batching, momentum, and Nesterov acceleration -- the optimizer substrate beneath Adam. IN: the update rules, why stochasticity helps and regularizes, momentum as an EMA of gradients, the noise scale. OUT: adaptive methods (link Adam and AdamW), LR schedules and gradient-noise-scale batch sizing at scale (link 04), at-scale optimizer engineering (link 04).
key_points: SGD update theta <- theta - eta*g; a mini-batch gradient is an unbiased estimate of the full gradient with variance ~ 1/B, giving diminishing returns to batch size past the critical batch size (McCandlish et al. 2018 gradient noise scale -- link 04)
Momentum: v <- mu*v + g, theta <- theta - eta*v; mu=0.9 averages over ~1/(1-mu)=10 recent gradients, damping oscillation across the short axis of ill-conditioned valleys
Nesterov evaluates the gradient at the look-ahead point theta - eta*mu*v; it improves the constant in convex theory but rarely matters in deep nets

SGD's implicit regularization: gradient noise biases the trajectory toward flat, low-norm minima, which is the leading explanation for why plain SGD often test-generalizes better than Adam on vision (link Generalization, Lore - The Adam vs SGD Generalization Wars)

The learning rate is the single most important hyperparameter: too high diverges to NaN, too low crawls or sticks; the LR range test (Smith 2015) sweeps LR upward until loss diverges to find the usable band

Non-obvious: the mu=0.9 default is folklore that happens to match typical curvature timescales (~10-step averaging); heavy-ball momentum is a discretized damped oscillator, and too-high mu can itself cause overshoot
links: Lore - The Adam vs SGD Generalization Wars

notes.title: Concept - Dropout
notes.scope: Dropout as stochastic regularization: random unit masking, inverted-dropout scaling, train/eval behavior, and the ensemble interpretation. IN: the mechanism, typical rates, why it regularizes, DropConnect/stochastic-depth variants, MC-dropout. OUT: weight decay as a regularizer (covered under Adam and AdamW), the BatchNorm/Dropout ordering pitfall as an aggregated gotcha (link Gotchas, Breakdown - Batch Normalization).
key_points: Inverted dropout: at train time zero each unit with probability p and scale survivors by 1/(1-p) so the expected activation is preserved; at test time do nothing. Forgetting the survivor scaling is a classic silent bug that shifts activation magnitude at inference
Interpretation: approximates an exponential ensemble of ~2^n weight-sharing subnetworks (Srivastava et al. 2014); equivalently an adaptive-noise injection that penalizes co-adaptation of features
Rates: 0.1-0.5 for MLPs/CNNs; transformers typically use ~0.1 (attention and residual dropout) and often 0.0 for large-model pretraining, where dataset scale supplies the regularization instead
Dropout and BatchNorm interact badly -- the variance shift between train (dropped) and eval (kept) statistics degrades accuracy (Li et al. 2019); LayerNorm-based transformers sidestep this
Variants: DropConnect drops weights not activations; stochastic depth / DropPath (Huang et al. 2016) drops whole residual branches and is key to training very deep ResNets and ViTs
Non-obvious: keeping dropout ON at inference and averaging many stochastic forward passes (MC-dropout, Gal-Ghahramani 2016) yields a cheap predictive-uncertainty estimate

notes.title: Concept - Embeddings as Learned Representations
notes.scope: Embedding layers as learned lookup tables and the geometry of representation space: token/positional/categorical embeddings, sparse gradients, weight tying, and distributed representations. IN: lookup mechanics, sparse-row gradients, tied input/output embeddings, embedding init and norm pathologies. OUT: embedding MODELS for retrieval (link 11), word2vec history (link 17), positional encodings/RoPE (link 03), feature superposition (link 14).
key_points: An embedding layer is a matrix E of shape (V, d); a lookup equals one_hot @ E, and the backward updates only the rows of tokens present in the batch -- a sparse gradient that needs sparse-aware optimizer handling

Weight tying (Press-Wolf 2017, Inan et al. 2016): share the input embedding with the output projection so E = W_out^T; saves V*d params (enormous for large vocab) and usually improves perplexity; used in GPT-2

Distributed representation: meaning lives in directions of a continuous space, not in single neurons; approximate linear structure emerges (king - man + woman ~ queen), and the LM head becomes a dot-product retrieval against token embeddings
Init folklore: GPT-family embeddings init ~ N(0, 0.02); the original Transformer multiplies embeddings by sqrt(d) to match sinusoidal positional-encoding magnitude
Failure: rare/undertrained token rows keep near-init norms while others grow, producing anomalous 'glitch tokens' like SolidGoldMagikarp that trigger degenerate behavior (link 18 Glitch Tokens)
Non-obvious: because meaning is superposed across more directions than there are neurons, individual embedding dimensions are rarely interpretable (link 14 Superposition)
links: Concept - Matrix Multiplication as the Atom of Deep Learning

notes.title: Snippet - A Minimal Training Loop in PyTorch
notes.scope: A complete, runnable training loop for a small MLP classifier that demonstrates correct operation ordering, train/eval switching, gradient clipping, and the param-group weight-decay split. IN: the ~40-line runnable example and the 3-4 expert decisions encoded in it. OUT: distributed/AMP scaling (link 04), the theory behind each component (link the concept notes).
key_points: Complete runnable code: synthetic dataset -> nn.Sequential MLP -> AdamW with two param groups -> loop: zero_grad(set_to_none=True), forward, cross_entropy, backward, clip_grad_norm_(1.0), step; plus a torch.no_grad() eval block toggled by model.eval()
Show the weight-decay param-group split exactly like nanoGPT's configure_optimizers: decay only 2D matmul weights, NO decay on biases, LayerNorm/RMSNorm gains, or embeddings
Show model.train()/model.eval() toggling and state why it matters (Dropout and BatchNorm behavior change)
Show gradient clipping positioned after backward() and before step(), and print grad norm to make spikes visible
Header block: deps (torch 2.x), expected output (loss falling from ~ln(num_classes) toward 0 on an overfittable batch), approximate runtime on CPU
Why-written-this-way: set_to_none memory/perf win and its None-vs-0 semantics, the decay param-group rationale, clip-before-step ordering, no_grad() in eval to free activation memory
links: Playbook - Debugging a Neural Network That Won't Train

notes.title: Concept - Adam and AdamW
notes.scope: The Adam optimizer and the AdamW decoupled-weight-decay fix: first/second moment EMAs, bias correction, the update rule, memory cost, and why AdamW is not Adam+L2. IN: full mechanism, hyperparameters, the decoupling argument, when Adam beats SGD. OUT: at-scale optimizer engineering and Muon/Shampoo/Lion (link 04), the epsilon/bias-correction numerical arcana (link Adam's Epsilon and Bias Correction), LR schedules (link 04).
key_points: Adam (Kingma-Ba 2015): m <- b1*m + (1-b1)*g, v <- b2*v + (1-b2)*g^2, bias-correct m_hat=m/(1-b1^t), v_hat=v/(1-b2^t), update theta <- theta - eta*m_hat/(sqrt(v_hat)+eps); a per-parameter adaptive step
Defaults b1=0.9, b2=0.999, eps=1e-8, but LLM pretraining commonly uses b2=0.95 for faster, more stable second-moment adaptation at large batch -- the '0.95 for transformers' folklore

AdamW (Loshchilov-Hutter 2019): apply weight decay as theta <- theta - eta*lambda*theta DECOUPLED from the gradient, not folded in as L2, because Adam's per-coordinate 1/sqrt(v) scaling distorts an L2 term's intended uniform shrinkage; AdamW is now the universal default (weight decay ~0.1)

Memory: Adam stores m and v, typically in fp32, i.e. 8 bytes/param on top of weights and gradient -- this dominates optimizer-state memory and is what ZeRO shards (link 08 Memory Math, 04 Data Parallelism and ZeRO)

The update magnitude is roughly bounded by eta because m_hat/sqrt(v_hat) ~ +/-1, making Adam behave like a smoothed sign-descent -- why Adam LRs (1e-4 to 1e-3) are small and transfer better than SGD LRs
Failure: Adam can settle in sharper minima that generalize worse than SGD (link Lore); Reddi et al. 2018 gave a convex non-convergence counterexample fixed by AMSGrad's max-of-v
links: Concept - Stochastic Gradient Descent and Momentum
Concept - Adam's Epsilon and Bias Correction
Lore - The Adam vs SGD Generalization Wars

notes.title: Concept - RMSNorm and LayerNorm
notes.scope: Layer Normalization and RMSNorm: per-token feature normalization, learnable gain/bias, why they stabilize training, and why RMSNorm (dropping mean-centering) won in modern LLMs. IN: both mechanisms, the gradient effect, the re-centering question, precision handling. OUT: pre-norm vs post-norm placement (link 03), BatchNorm (link Breakdown), the which-norm decision (link Decision).
key_points: LayerNorm (Ba et al. 2016): normalize over the feature dim per token, x_hat = (x - mean)/sqrt(var + eps), then scale-shift gamma*x_hat + beta; batch-independent, so it works for variable-length sequences, RNNs, and transformers where BatchNorm fails

RMSNorm (Zhang-Sennrich 2019): drop mean subtraction and bias, x/sqrt(mean(x^2) + eps) * gamma; ~7-64% faster on the norm op (no mean, no beta) and used in LLaMA/T5/most modern LLMs -- empirical evidence the re-centering was unnecessary

Why it stabilizes: rescaling activations to a fixed magnitude keeps the forward pass scale-invariant to its input and keeps gradients well-conditioned across depth, decoupling layers during optimization

Precision: LayerNorm/RMSNorm are computed in fp32 even under bf16/fp16 mixed precision, because the sum-of-squares variance underflows in low precision (link 04 Mixed Precision Training, 01 Floating Point)
eps placement (1e-5 vs 1e-6) and whether gamma is initialized to 1.0 are load-bearing details; some models drop the learnable bias entirely

Non-obvious: the LayerNorm backward is not a simple rescale -- its gradient subtracts the mean and the projection onto x, removing the gradient component along the activation direction, which is part of why it conditions optimization
links: Concept - Floating Point for Deep Learning

notes.title: Concept - Weight Initialization
notes.scope: Why initial weight scale decides whether a deep net trains at all, and the variance-preserving schemes plus transformer-specific residual scaling. IN: the variance-preservation argument, Xavier/He/LeCun/orthogonal formulas, fan-in/out, residual-scaled init, symmetry breaking. OUT: the full formula lookup (folded into this note's table), normalization as a partial substitute (link norm notes), at-scale muP init (link 04).
key_points: Goal: keep the per-layer variance of activations (forward) and gradients (backward) near 1 so signals neither vanish nor explode exponentially with depth
Xavier/Glorot (2010): Var(W) = 2/(fan_in + fan_out), derived for tanh/linear; He/Kaiming (2015): Var(W) = 2/fan_in for ReLU, where the factor 2 compensates for ReLU zeroing half the variance
LeCun init (1/fan_in) for SELU/self-normalizing nets; orthogonal init exactly preserves vector norms and helps RNNs and very deep linear-ish stacks

Transformers: init ~ N(0, 0.02) (GPT-2) and additionally scale residual-projection weights by 1/sqrt(2N) with N = layer count, so the additive residual stream's variance does not grow linearly with depth -- the GPT-2 'scale the residual projections' trick

Bias init 0 (except the LSTM forget-gate bias ~1.0 folklore to keep the gate open early); norm gain init 1.0; identical/symmetric init makes all units in a layer compute the same function forever because gradients stay identical -- symmetry never breaks

Non-obvious: BatchNorm/LayerNorm make a network far more forgiving of init scale, so normalization partially substitutes for careful init -- and norm-free nets (Fixup/NF-Net) must re-introduce precise init to compensate (link Normalization-Free Networks)
links: Concept - Floating Point for Deep Learning

notes.title: Concept - Vanishing and Exploding Gradients
notes.scope: Why gradients shrink or blow up multiplicatively through depth and time, how it manifests, and the toolkit that fixes it. IN: the Jacobian-product/spectral-radius mechanism, symptoms and detection, and the fix stack (init, norm, residuals, clipping, gating). OUT: each fix's own note (init, norm, residuals, clipping in the loop), LSTM/GRU gating detail (link 03 RNN lineage), SSM stability (link 03).
key_points: Backprop multiplies Jacobians across layers, so the gradient norm scales like the product of per-layer spectral norms; typical singular values below 1 vanish, above 1 explode -- both exponential in depth or sequence length
Saturating activations (sigmoid deriv <= 0.25) compound vanishing; this is the mechanistic reason deep nets and vanilla RNNs would not train before ~2010 (Hochreiter 1991, Bengio et al. 1994)

Symptoms and detection: early-layer grad norms orders of magnitude below late-layer norms (vanish) or NaN/Inf and loss spikes (explode); log per-layer grad-norm ratios and watch the LR-warmup boundary where spikes cluster (link 04 training stability, z-loss)

Fix stack: variance-preserving init, ReLU-family activations, normalization layers, residual connections (an identity path gives gradients a highway), global-norm gradient clipping, and gating (LSTM/GRU) for recurrence

Residual connections do not remove bad Jacobians -- they ADD an identity term so the product stays ~1 (the I + F' structure), which is the concrete reason ResNets train at 1000+ layers (link Residual Connections)
Non-obvious: exploding gradients in transformers often trace to attention-logit growth and unclipped updates rather than the FFN; clipping plus lower LR at warmup is the standard mitigation
links: Concept - State Space Models and Mamba

notes.title: Concept - Residual Connections
notes.scope: Skip/residual connections as the gradient highway that makes very deep nets trainable: the identity-mapping mechanism, gradient flow, and the residual-stream view. IN: the y = x + F(x) mechanism, why gradients survive, pre-activation ordering, the additive-stream interpretation, depth-variance scaling. OUT: pre-norm vs post-norm placement (link 03), ResNet-as-CNN-architecture detail (link 03), residual-stream interpretability circuits (link 14).
key_points: y = x + F(x) gives backward dL/dx = dL/dy * (I + F'(x)); the identity term guarantees gradient reaches early layers even when F'(x) ~ 0 (He et al. 2015/2016), directly countering vanishing gradients

It solves the degradation problem: plain deep nets get WORSE with added depth (not from overfitting) because they cannot even learn to approximate identity; residuals make identity the zero-effort default
Pre-activation ordering (He 2016) -- norm/activation before the weight -- yields a cleaner unobstructed identity path; the transformer analog is pre-norm placement (link 03)

Residual-stream view: in transformers each block reads from and writes additively to a shared stream that acts as a memory bus; interpretability treats it as the substrate where features are written and read (link 14 Induction Heads)
Depth scaling: because contributions are summed, residual-stream variance grows ~ linearly with depth, requiring 1/sqrt(2N) init or normalization to control (link Weight Initialization)
Non-obvious: a deep residual net behaves like an ensemble of many shorter paths (Veit et al. 2016) -- deleting a single residual layer barely hurts, unlike a plain net where it is catastrophic

notes.title: Concept - Generalization in Deep Learning
notes.scope: Why overparameterized nets generalize despite the capacity to memorize noise: the classical-vs-modern picture, flat minima, implicit regularization, and effective capacity. IN: the rethinking-generalization result, flat-vs-sharp minima, SGD's implicit bias, norm/margin bounds. OUT: grokking and double descent as named phenomena (link 18), sharpness-aware training as a method (link SAM), scaling laws (link 04).
key_points: Zhang et al. 2017 'Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization': nets fit random labels to zero training error yet still generalize on real labels, so classical VC/capacity bounds cannot explain what is happening

Flat minima generalize better (Hochreiter-Schmidhuber 1997, Keskar et al. 2017): large-batch training finds sharper minima that generalize worse; the flatness-generalization link is contested in detail but load-bearing in practice

Implicit regularization: SGD's gradient noise and its optimization trajectory bias solutions toward low-norm, flat regions even with no explicit regularizer -- much of generalization comes from the optimizer, not the loss
Effective capacity is not parameter count; norm-based and margin-based bounds (Bartlett et al. 2017) correlate with generalization far better than VC dimension
In the overparameterized regime more parameters can REDUCE test error past the interpolation threshold, contradicting the classical U-curve (link 18 Double Descent)
Non-obvious: explicit regularizers (dropout, weight decay) are often neither necessary nor sufficient for good generalization here -- they help but the implicit bias of training does much of the work
links: Concept - Stochastic Gradient Descent and Momentum

notes.title: Breakdown - Batch Normalization
notes.scope: Reverse-engineering BatchNorm: what the 2015 paper claimed, what the mechanism actually is, the internal-covariate-shift myth, the train/eval discrepancy, and batch-size dependence. IN: the algorithm, running stats, the ICS debunking, loss-landscape smoothing, why it fails at small batch and in transformers. OUT: LayerNorm/RMSNorm (link their note), the which-norm decision (link Decision), general regularization theory.
key_points: Headline: BatchNorm (Ioffe-Szegedy 2015) let CNNs train with much higher learning rates and converge faster on ImageNet; it became near-universal in vision until transformers moved to LayerNorm
How it works: normalize each feature over the BATCH dimension using batch mean/variance at train time, maintain EMA running stats (momentum default 0.1) for eval, then apply learnable gamma/beta

The clever-but-wrong part: the paper attributed its benefit to reducing 'internal covariate shift', but Santurkar et al. 2018 showed ICS is largely unchanged and BatchNorm instead SMOOTHS the loss landscape (improves gradient Lipschitzness) -- a famous case of the right technique with the wrong stated mechanism
Train/eval discrepancy: batch stats in train vs running stats in eval means small batches, distribution shift, or a forgotten model.eval() silently collapse accuracy -- a top production bug

Batch-size dependence and leakage: statistics get noisy at batch size 1-2 (so detection/segmentation and transformers use GroupNorm/LayerNorm), and normalizing over the batch leaks information across examples, a correctness hazard in some setups (e.g. contrastive/metric learning)
What to steal: the normalize-then-affine template and the higher-LR enablement; what to avoid: BatchNorm in transformers/RNNs and in any tiny-batch or cross-example-sensitive regime

notes.scope: A lookup sheet of optimizer update equations, default hyperparameters, and per-parameter memory cost, from SGD through AdamW. OUT: at-scale optimizers Muon/Shampoo/Lion/Adafactor engineering (link 04), the derivations and intuition (link the concept notes).

notes.title: Decision - Choosing a Normalization Layer
notes.scope: A framework for choosing among BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, GroupNorm, and no-norm, by architecture, batch size, and modality. IN: the decision flow and a tradeoff matrix with real numbers; the edge cases that flip the default. OUT: the mechanisms themselves (link norm notes, Breakdown - Batch Normalization), pre/post-norm placement (link 03).
key_points: Decision flow: transformer/sequence model -> LayerNorm or RMSNorm (RMSNorm if you want the speed win and are following LLaMA); large-batch CNN -> BatchNorm; small-batch vision such as detection/segmentation -> GroupNorm; want to drop norm entirely -> NF-Net-style adaptive gradient clipping (link Normalization-Free Networks)

Tradeoff matrix (options x criteria): batch dependence, train/eval discrepancy, per-op speed, cross-example leakage, extra params (beta) -- with numbers, e.g. RMSNorm removes the mean and beta and is measurably faster than LayerNorm on the norm op

Flip factors: batch size 1-2 rules out BatchNorm; variable sequence length rules out BatchNorm; RL/distillation fine-tuning where train/eval statistic mismatch bites favors batch-independent norms; kernel-fusion availability on your hardware can decide LN vs RMSNorm
Default for LLMs (as of 2026): RMSNorm in pre-norm placement (placement itself is owned by 03); default for classic CNNs: BatchNorm
Non-obvious: 'no norm' is viable but shifts the burden to precise init and gradient clipping, and has not been shown to scale to frontier LLMs (link Normalization-Free Networks)

notes.title: Playbook - Debugging a Neural Network That Won't Train
notes.scope: An operational procedure for diagnosing a model that will not learn, distilled from Karpathy's 'Recipe for Training Neural Networks' and lab practice. IN: ordered diagnostic steps from data inspection through overfit-a-batch to LR sweeps, with a symptom-to-cause branch table. OUT: the mechanism behind each fix (link the concept notes), distributed-training-specific debugging (link 04).
key_points: Step 1: verify loss at init (~ln(C) for C-class classification); a wrong value means a label, logit, or loss-reduction bug -- fix it before touching the model
Step 2: overfit a single batch to ~0 loss; if you cannot, the model or optimization is broken, not the data volume or regularization
Step 3: inspect the actual decoded inputs and targets entering the loss (catch preprocessing, off-by-one label shift, and tokenization bugs -- most 'model' bugs are data bugs)
Step 4: run an LR sweep / range test; disable fancy schedules first; NaN means LR/eps/overflow too high, a flat loss means LR too low or a disconnected graph
Step 5: turn OFF dropout, weight decay, and augmentation while debugging, then re-add once it trains -- regularizing before the model can fit masks the real problem
Step 6: check per-layer grad norms (vanishing/exploding), the dead-ReLU fraction, and that zero_grad and train/eval mode are correct

Branch table: NaN loss -> LR/eps/fp16 overflow; loss flat -> LR too low or graph disconnected; train good but val bad -> overfit or eval-mode/running-stats bug; loss falls then explodes -> clip gradients and lower LR at warmup

notes.title: Concept - The Edge of Stability
notes.scope: The empirical finding that gradient descent trains at a sharpness of ~2/eta rather than below it, contradicting classical descent-lemma intuition. IN: the 2/eta threshold, progressive sharpening, non-monotone loss, the adaptive-optimizer analog, and the LR-curvature-generalization link. OUT: classical convex convergence theory (link 01 optimization), sharpness-aware training as a method (link SAM), at-scale training stability (link 04).
key_points: Classical theory says GD converges only if sharpness (top Hessian eigenvalue lambda_max) < 2/eta; Cohen et al. 2021 showed real training instead DRIVES lambda_max up to ~2/eta and then hovers there -- the 'edge of stability'

Progressive sharpening: lambda_max rises throughout training until it hits 2/eta, after which the loss decreases NON-monotonically (it oscillates) yet still trends down, violating the monotone descent lemma

Implication: the usable learning rate is coupled to curvature -- the LR you pick sets the sharpness the model equilibrates at, linking LR directly to implicit flatness and thus generalization (link Generalization)
Adaptive optimizers have an analog (Cohen et al. 2022): Adam operates at an edge of stability measured in its preconditioned norm, so the phenomenon is not specific to plain GD

Why it matters practically: it explains why LR warmup helps (it lets sharpness adjust before the full LR hits), why some 'too large' LRs work anyway, and why smaller LRs can find flatter, better-generalizing solutions
Folklore/open (as of 2026): the precise interaction of the edge of stability with SGD minibatch noise, batch size, and normalization is unsettled
links: Concept - Stochastic Gradient Descent and Momentum

notes.title: Concept - Sharpness-Aware Minimization
notes.scope: SAM: minimizing the worst-case loss within a neighborhood to bias training toward flat minima, its two-step gradient, cost, and variants. IN: the min-max objective, the ascend-then-descend update, ASAM and efficiency variants, empirical gains and the 2x-cost barrier. OUT: the flatness-generalization theory (link Generalization), the edge-of-stability view of curvature (link Edge of Stability), at-scale training (link 04).
key_points: Objective (Foret et al. 2020): minimize max over ||eps|| <= rho of L(theta + eps), pushing toward flat minima; approximated by an ascent step to theta + rho*g/||g|| followed by a gradient step evaluated at that perturbed point

Cost: two forward-backward passes per step (one to find the worst-case point, one to update), which is the main adoption barrier; LookSAM and applying SAM every k steps recover most of the gain more cheaply
rho (the neighborhood radius, ~0.05) is the key hyperparameter; ASAM (Kwon et al. 2021) makes it scale-invariant so it transfers across layers with different weight norms
Gains: consistent test-accuracy and robustness improvements on vision (ResNet, ViT), largest where data is limited or the model would otherwise overfit

Connection: SAM explicitly optimizes for the flatness that plain SGD only achieves implicitly, making it a controlled probe of the flatness-generalization hypothesis (link Generalization, Edge of Stability)
Open/folklore (as of 2026): whether SAM's benefit justifies the 2x compute at LLM-pretraining scale is unclear; it remains mostly a vision and fine-tuning tool
links: Concept - Stochastic Gradient Descent and Momentum

notes.title: Concept - Normalization-Free Networks
notes.scope: Training deep nets without normalization layers: why you would want to, and the techniques -- scaled residuals, adaptive gradient clipping, near-zero residual init -- that replace BatchNorm/LayerNorm. IN: NF-Nets, adaptive gradient clipping, Fixup/SkipInit/ReZero, DeepNorm, and what norm's real jobs are. OUT: the norm layers themselves (link norm notes), the which-norm decision (link Decision), pre/post-norm placement (link 03).
key_points: Motivation: BatchNorm carries a train/eval discrepancy, cross-batch information leakage, and a compute/memory cost; removing normalization improves throughput and reproducibility if you can keep training stable

NF-Nets (Brock et al. 2021): scaled residual blocks plus Adaptive Gradient Clipping (clip each gradient by a ratio to its weight norm) match or beat BatchNorm ResNets on ImageNet at higher training throughput

Fixup (Zhang et al. 2019), SkipInit, and ReZero (Bachlechner et al. 2020): initialize each residual branch near zero (e.g. a learnable scalar starting at 0) so the network begins as identity and can train deep with no norm

Mechanism: these methods reproduce norm's two real jobs -- controlling residual-stream variance growth with depth and keeping gradients well-scaled -- through init and clipping instead of runtime normalization

Transformers: fully norm-free transformers are hard because norm placement is load-bearing for stability; most keep RMSNorm, and DeepNet/DeepNorm scales the residual branch (allowing 1000-layer transformers) rather than removing norm (link 04 training stability)
Open (as of 2026): whether norm-free approaches scale to frontier LLMs is unresolved -- RMSNorm remains the default

notes.title: Gotchas - Training Neural Networks
notes.scope: The aggregated catalog of training bugs and silent failures practitioners learn the hard way -- data, loss, optimizer, precision, and mode bugs -- ranked by how much pain they cause. IN: symptom/cause/fix/detection for each pitfall. OUT: the mechanisms in depth (link the concept notes), distributed/at-scale-specific gotchas (link 04).
key_points: Forgot zero_grad: gradients accumulate across steps so loss stalls or explodes; detection = grad norm grows every step. Fix = zero_grad(set_to_none=True) before each backward

Loss-reduction mismatch: sum vs mean vs per-token silently rescales the effective LR by batch/sequence length; the masked-loss token-count bug undercounts valid tokens in SFT (link 06). Detection = loss magnitude jumps when batch size changes

Wrong train/eval mode: BatchNorm running stats keep updating or Dropout stays active at eval, giving nondeterministic or degraded metrics; forgetting model.eval() is a top production incident (link Breakdown - Batch Normalization)
Data not shuffled, label leakage, or train/test contamination: too-good validation then production collapse (link 13 Benchmark Contamination). Detection = suspiciously fast val improvement
NaN loss: log(0) in a hand-rolled loss, fp16 overflow in exp/softmax, LR too high, or bad init; detection = assert torch.isfinite(loss) and check loss-at-init ~ ln(C) (link 01 Floating Point)
Regularizing before fitting: augmentation/dropout/weight-decay turned on before the model can overfit a single batch masks the real bug (link Playbook)
Silent autograd breaks: an in-place op, a .detach(), or reusing a graph across steps zeroes or errors the backward; set_to_none changes None-vs-0 semantics some code relies on
Non-obvious: the fastest triage for a mysterious 'model' failure is to decode and eyeball the exact tensors entering the loss -- pipeline bugs outnumber modeling bugs

notes.title: Lore - The Adam vs SGD Generalization Wars
notes.scope: The decade-long practitioner argument over whether adaptive optimizers generalize worse than SGD, why vision stayed on SGD while NLP embraced Adam, and how AdamW plus large-scale pretraining mostly ended the debate. IN: the narrative, the key papers and hacks, the resolution and its residue. OUT: the optimizer mechanisms (link Adam, SGD notes), at-scale optimizer engineering (link 04).
key_points: What happened: around 2017 Wilson et al. 'The Marginal Value of Adaptive Gradient Methods' argued SGD generalizes better than Adam on vision; ImageNet SOTA stayed on SGD+momentum for years while transformers and NLP defaulted to Adam
SWATS (Keskar-Socher 2017): a shipped hack that starts with Adam for speed and switches to SGD late for generalization -- people really ran this to get both
The plot twist: AdamW (Loshchilov-Hutter 2019) showed much of Adam's 'bad generalization' was actually improperly coupled weight decay; decoupling it closed most of the reported gap

Why NLP/transformers effectively require Adam: sparse, heavy-tailed gradients from embeddings and LayerNorm and very large condition numbers make SGD impractical, and transformer loss landscapes differ from CNNs (link Embeddings, RMSNorm and LayerNorm)

Resolution (as of 2026): AdamW is the universal LLM default, SGD survives in parts of vision and some fine-tuning, and the 'Adam generalizes worse' claim is now read mostly as a weight-decay artifact -- though the flat-minima intuition persists
Evidence status: well-sourced on the papers and hacks; the 'transformers just can't use SGD' explanation is a folklore layer that is directionally true but rarely rigorously stated
links: Concept - Stochastic Gradient Descent and Momentum

notes.title: Concept - Adam's Epsilon and Bias Correction
notes.scope: The numerical arcana of Adam that only bites at scale: where epsilon sits, why 1e-8 breaks in low precision, the bias-correction/warmup interaction, and RAdam. IN: epsilon placement, precision underflow, bias-correction-vs-warmup, beta2 memory, the sign-descent bound. OUT: the base Adam mechanism (link Adam and AdamW), mixed-precision engineering (link 04), general hyperparameter folklore (link 18).
key_points: Epsilon placement: Adam adds eps OUTSIDE the sqrt as m_hat/(sqrt(v_hat)+eps), whereas LAMB and some variants put it inside as m_hat/sqrt(v_hat+eps); when v_hat is tiny these differ substantially -- a silent cross-framework reproducibility trap

Precision: default eps=1e-8 can round away or underflow in fp16 (smallest normal ~6e-5), so optimizer states are kept in an fp32 master copy; large-model configs raise eps to 1e-6 or even 1e-5 for stability (the 'raise Adam eps for big models' folklore)
Bias correction is largest early -- for beta2=0.999 the second moment needs ~1/(1-beta2)=2000 steps to warm up; without correction the first thousands of steps take biased, too-small effective steps

Bias correction and LR warmup partly do the same job; RAdam (Liu et al. 2019) frames warmup as a variance-reduction fix for Adam's early high-variance adaptive term and rectifies it automatically until enough samples accumulate
beta2 choice: 0.999 (~2000-step memory) vs 0.95 (~20-step) -- large-batch LLMs use 0.95 for faster, more stable adaptation, and this interacts with eps and with gradient clipping at warmup

Non-obvious: because m_hat/sqrt(v_hat) ~ +/-1, Adam's per-step update magnitude is roughly bounded by the LR, making it behave like smoothed sign descent -- the reason Adam LRs are tiny and far more transferable across scales than SGD LRs
